job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Wendy Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I walk to work from a rented room above a hairdresser's in Alder Bridge. I'm a trainee assistant at a small accounting practice, Bianchi and Daughters. I started in July after my accounting degree. I file tax returns for small shops and farms, check receipts against bank statements and answer the phone. I like that every day looks the same. In the evenings I sit with my professional exam books and a cup of tea, and I try not to look at my loan balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I like things steady. Our practice uses the same software it did ten years ago and clients like seeing a real person. I'd tell my friends there's no need to rush at anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still have worries, but they're about money. My room costs more than I'd like, my loan comes out on the first, and I'm on a trainee wage. If a client leaves or Mr Bianchi has a bad year, I'm the one he can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd sit my first professional exam in the spring, keep the room, and get through each month. I wouldn't try any AI tool, because I've never needed one and I'd worry about mistakes on a client's return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A quiet worry about money, like a tap dripping in another room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mr Bianchi having a bad year. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly. Two of his bigger clients have been asking about cheaper online services. He says they always come back, but he looks tired when he says it. I don't want to think about it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the practice had to let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for another firm like it, though there are only three in town. I'd probably have to move to the city and share a room, which I'd hate. I like knowing where the bakery is and which bus I need.

say: Our practice has used the same software for **ten years** and clients like a real person.
There's no need to **rush** at anything new.
think: My worry is **money**: rent, the loan on the first and a trainee wage.
If Mr Bianchi (my boss) has a bad year, I'm the one he **can't afford**.
do: Sit my first **professional exam** in the spring and get through each month.
Avoid AI tools, as a mistake on a client's **return** would be on me.
feel: Mostly fine, with a quiet worry like a **dripping tap**.
S0.quote: I like knowing where the bakery is and which bus I need.
fieldNote: Prefers **routine** and ties her sense of safety to her small town.
Her worry is the practice's **finances**, not technology.
Only three firms nearby, so a job loss would mean **moving**.

steps.text: Sit the first professional accounting exam in the spring
Keep the rented room and pay the loan on time each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's worrying for clerks but we're fine because tax is a trust business. I'd tell people the practice will be okay because small clients want to see a face, although I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it hits exactly what I do. Checking receipts, matching statements and filing standard returns are the sort of thing software can do. Mr Bianchi's daughters might decide that two trainees are one too many. I'm the newer one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get good at the parts that need judgement, like explaining a return to a nervous farmer. I'd keep studying for the exam. I wouldn't jump to try the new software unless Mr Bianchi told me to, and then I'd learn it slowly with someone checking my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like the ground I stand on is a bit softer than yesterday, and I can't say where it'll give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start using the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Bianchi brought them in and showed me step by step. I don't want to be the one who finds a button and sends a wrong figure to the tax office. I'm happy to be second, even third, if it means being right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in being slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. If the others are twice as quick, I look like a problem. My friend Livia says I should try it on my own time. I can see the sense, but I get a knot in my stomach when I think about it.

I tell people the practice will be okay, though I'm **not sure**.

steps.text: Keep studying for the exam on weeknights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too quickly and the government should step in. Two years is no time. I'd tell friends to be careful with savings, if they have any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I can't picture it. My job is exactly the kind of work a machine would do cheaper. I'd have maybe a year and a half of being useful. I have a thin purse, a pass degree and no internship, and I'm someone who finds change hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra, and I'd ask my mother whether I could come home if it went badly, even though she lives three hours away and has no space. I'd try to finish the exam anyway, in case it matters. I'd probably ask Mr Bianchi what he plans to do and then wait to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frozen, if I'm honest. I'm the sort who sits still when a car is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you find change hard. What would be the first practical step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a list. I like lists. Rent, loan, food, and what I can drop. Then a second list of every job I could apply for. I wouldn't do anything fast, but I'd write everything down so it feels less like a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Livia, who's more confident than I am. And my gran. She lived through a factory closing, and she says that you survive by having a little money and being kind to your neighbours. That sounds old-fashioned, but it comforts me.

say: Two years is **too quick**, and government must step in.
I'd tell friends to be careful with **savings**, if they have any.
think: My job is the kind a machine does **cheaper**, so I'd have about a year and a half.
With a thin purse and a pass degree, I find **change** hard.
do: Stop all **extra spending** and finish the exam in case it matters.

feel: **Frozen**, like someone who sits still when a car is coming.
S2.quote: I'm the sort who sits still when a car is coming.
fieldNote: Freezes under pressure: has no **plan** and little money to make one.
Her coping tool is **lists**, which she offers without prompting.
Takes comfort from her **gran**, who lived through a factory closing.

steps.text: Cut every extra and write down rent, loan and food costs
Ask my mother if I can move home if it goes badly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us time, but nobody I know is using that time. I'd tell friends to get a trade or at least a second string. I'd be talking about it, but not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like a count-down I'd rather not look at. I'd be 27, and by then probably senior enough to have my own clients, or the job's gone. I'd like to think it's the first, but I wouldn't bet money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the professional exam and try to be the one Mr Bianchi trusts with the difficult clients. I'd save a small amount every month, even 30, and learn the one tool that the practice picks. I'd also start going to a local evening class for something practical, like bookkeeping for small farms, which a person would still want to talk through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the two-year one, but not calm. I'd have a clock ticking and a plan in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a plan in a drawer. What's in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three jobs I could do if the practice closed: a bank counter, a farm office, or training as a teaching assistant. None pays well, but they all need a person. I haven't told Mr Bianchi, because it feels disloyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part of acting on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting. I'm slow to leave something that works. I'd probably wait too long, and I know it. That's the part I'd have to fight in myself.

say: Five years gives us time, but nobody I know is **using it**.
I'd tell friends to learn a **trade** or second string, without shouting.
think: At 27 I'd either have **my own clients** or the job would be gone.
Five years feels like a **countdown** I'd rather not look at.
do: Finish the exam and become the trainee Mr Bianchi trusts with **difficult clients**.
Save **30 a month** and take an evening class in farm bookkeeping.
feel: Calmer than the two-year case, but with a **clock ticking**.

fieldNote: Has a **fallback list** but feels disloyal telling her boss.

steps.text: Pass the exam and ask Mr Bianchi for the harder clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no reason to panic. I'd tell friends to carry on, save and get qualified. I'd probably sound calmer than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's easier. I'd be 32 with a qualification, maybe a house deposit, and a few years of clients behind me. I'd still feel the pull to stay put and not learn anything new, but ten years gives me time to be dragged along without drowning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through the exams and stay at the practice. I'd learn the practice's tools only when they arrive. I'd start paying the loan down faster after two years, and save towards a one-bedroom flat in Alder Bridge. I might look into advisory work for small farms, which depends on knowing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It feels like an ordinary life with a long weather forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part of the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeping up when the tools change. I've watched Mr Bianchi struggle with new screens, and I'm like him. But I'd learn if I had to, even if slowly. The danger is deciding too late that I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone younger than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't borrow as much as I did, and pick somewhere where you know people. A small town doesn't pay much but it holds you up when things go wrong.

say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no reason to **panic**.
I'd tell friends to carry on, save and get **qualified**.
think: At 32 I'd have a **qualification**, maybe a deposit and years of clients.
I'd still feel the pull to **stay put**, but a decade lets me be dragged along.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd freeze and have no money. What would help is a proper safety net and help finding another job that isn't just an online form. A named person at an office who could say, here's what you do next. And time to learn new things at work rather than on my own evenings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against new things. I like things that have been tested. People say that means I'm afraid, and sometimes it does. But I'd rather be sure than quick, and I wish the world would let people like me be that.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things. I like things that have been tested.
portrait: Wendy is a **22-year-old** trainee at a small accounting practice in Alder Bridge, renting a room above a hairdresser's.
She has a heavy loan, a thin purse and a strong liking for **routine and small-town life**.
She never uses AI and learns new software only with **supervision**.
Her fears centre on the practice's finances and the three-firm job market, more than on technology itself.
She goes from anxious in the slow case to **panicked** in the two-year case, then eases with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would freeze with no money and few local jobs.
whatWouldHelp: A **named person** at an office guiding her to the next job, plus a safety net and paid learning time.
